spoken: October the twenty-second, nineteen sixty-two. Surulere, Lagos. A borrowed school building, ceiling fans turning slow, chalk dust hanging in the light. Somewhere outside, the lagoon is breathing. This morning, a university says its first word.
But to understand that morning, we must widen our lens, to a newborn nation, hungry for its own people. This is the story of the University of Lagos, as it happened. In deed. And in truth.
truth: TITLE/FACT (motto is factual; framing sentence is authorial but non-factual).

spoken: First, picture Lagos in nineteen sixty, Eko, as Lagos is known at home; a lagoon city, a federal capital, streets loud with possibility. On the first of October, independence came, and the green-white-green rose over a country of many nations. A new flag. A new anthem. And already, a familiar ache: the country had more dreams than hands.

Years before, education had moved carefully. Yaba Higher College had trained a precious few. University College Ibadan, from nineteen forty-eight, had opened the doors of degree study, and still, the numbers never matched the need. Doctors. Engineers. Lawyers. Teachers. Everywhere the nation looked, it found empty chairs where professionals should be.

So the nation went looking for its own answer. In nineteen fifty-nine and sixty, the Ashby Commission weighed Nigeria's manpower needs in a report called Investment in Education, and the maths was blunt: the country needed many more trained professionals, fast. The question now was not why, but how. And the answer would arrive by law.
truth: CONTEXT-VERIFY (Ashby report is real and named; all visuals are graphic treatments).

spoken: Treat the paper like a character, because it is one. The University of Lagos Act, Number Eleven of nineteen sixty-two, passed by the Federal Parliament as an immediate answer to a national need: professionals, to drive social, economic and political development. One sheet of law. And inside it, a whole institution waiting to be born.

On the fifth of June, nineteen sixty-two, the Provisional Council was inaugurated, eleven members, charged with building a university long before any campus stood. Below them, a Senate would steer academic affairs, in the manner of universities everywhere. Structure, before stones. It is not glamour. It is how serious institutions begin.
truth: FACT (narration); visual is RECONSTRUCTION-flavoured because no photos of that sitting are in our ledger — the on-screen tag **Illustrative image** carries it.

spoken: And the Act held a surprise. It created not one body, but two: the Main University, and a separate Council for a Medical School at the teaching hospital in Idi-Araba. Born as twins. Two institutions, one name. Remember that; it will shape everything.

Every ship like this needs a helmsman. He came from Ebem, in Ohafia, Eni Njoku, born on the sixth of November, nineteen seventeen. A botanist by training, shaped at the University of Manchester. A man who had spent years at University College, Ibadan, teaching botany from nineteen forty-eight. A professor. And now, a pioneer.

In nineteen sixty-two, Eni Njoku became the university's first Vice-Chancellor, the first of thirteen, as the years would prove. So far, his university existed mostly on paper: a name, a law, a council, and borrowed rooms. Its motto already knew the standard it must meet, In deed and in truth. Not what you claim. What you do. Concrete would come later. First, mornings.

Morning in Surulere. A young clerk, newly admitted, buttons his only good shirt. Somewhere a kettle sings; a neighbour is already late. He walks into a corridor that has never heard a university lecture, and takes the seat that changes his life.

On the twenty-second of October, nineteen sixty-two, about three weeks after the nation's second independence anniversary, the first lectures were heard. Law: fifty-six students. Business and Social Studies: forty-six. The Medical School: twenty-eight. About one hundred and thirty in all; the university's own page says one hundred and thirty-one. And notice one more detail: the faculty began as Commerce and Business Administration, renamed Business and Social Studies at its Board's very first meeting. Two sites, one dawn: Surulere, and Idi-Araba, where tomorrow's doctors were already scrubbing in.
truth: FACT (all narration); visuals: tableaux are Reconstruction-tagged.

spoken: Word spreads. By nineteen sixty-four, the timetable could not contain the demand: four new faculties, Arts, Education, Engineering, Science, joined the original three. Students multiplied. Lecture rooms were borrowed, squeezed, shared. The university was outgrowing the temporary home that sheltered it. It needed ground of its own.

Down by the lagoon, at Akoka, the answer was rising into the sky. By nineteen sixty-five, the first phase stood complete. Count it, block by block: the Academic Group, North and South. The Dining Hall. The Library. The Administrative Block. The Central Concourse. Staff quarters. Student hostels. Brick by brick, blueprints had turned into a place with a pulse.

Then, colour. The sepia lifts, and Akoka opens in gold and teal: dawn light moving down the new concrete, a campus breathing its first full breath. Borrowed rooms, farewell. This was home now. And with home came the harder work: becoming one university.

Growth asked a governance question. In nineteen sixty-seven, the University of Lagos Decree, Number Three of that year, answered it: one Council for the whole university. The Medical School became the College of Medicine, keeping its own collegiate system. Two twins, in the end, one household.

On the twenty-eighth of June, nineteen seventy-three, the Senate adopted the faculty system for the whole university, the College of Medicine standing apart, in its collegiate tradition. The following year, General Gowon came, in his capacity as Visitor, and signed the visitors' book, his remarks there in his own hand. Different pens, one story.

Nineteen eighty-one: the School of Postgraduate Studies, students nicknamed it the Lagoon Lighthouse. The International School was founded that same year, moving to its permanent site in October nineteen eighty-five. Nineteen eighty-four: the Senate House Complex, complete.

Then came a test no faculty had prepared for: a name. On the twenty-ninth of May, twenty twelve, Democracy Day, President Goodluck Jonathan's broadcast announced that UNILAG would be renamed Moshood Abiola University, honouring Chief M.K.O. Abiola, who died in detention in nineteen ninety-eight, and the democratic hope he had come to embody.

The response was immediate. Students, alumni and others poured onto the streets in protest; the matter went to court. Their core argument was simple: the university was created by an Act of Parliament, so a broadcast alone could not rename it. In time, a court agreed; and the reversal was reported in February twenty-thirteen.

Bring both truths to the table, because both are true. Abiola's legacy deserves a nation's respect. A university born by law has the right to defend its identity. Neither truth cancels the other, they stand side by side. Which is, in the end, what universities are for.
truth: FACT (evenhanded landing is authored but fair; no quids).

spoken: Today, walk the ground and count the proof. Twelve faculties. Three campuses, Akoka, Yaba, Idi-Araba. Thirteen Vice-Chancellors since Njoku, and the thirteenth, Professor Folasade Ogunsola, the first woman to hold the office. Enterprise has its own wings: UNILAG Consult, UNILAG Ventures. Research kept reaching, too. In later years, the record does not give the exact date, a Hydraulic Research Laboratory rose, with support from the Government of the Netherlands and thirty thousand naira from the Nigerian Ports Authority.

Today, count the years with me: sixty-four years since a borrowed classroom in Surulere heard its first lecture. The lamp we lit at the start never went out. It became the Lagoon Lighthouse. It rose, every morning, over the lagoon. University of First Choice, and the Nation's Pride. In deed. And in truth.
